result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_in_degree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get the in-degree of a node (directed graphs only). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L26132-L26206){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_in_degree(node) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![In-degree of one node](/assets/graphs/get-in-degree.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node directed graph with the queried node C outlined. The three arrows pointing into C, from A, B and E, are drawn in accent; the arrows C sends to B and D are not counted. The card reads in-degree 3." width="100%"} In-degree is the number of edges pointing into the node. Only meaningful for directed graphs. In-degree tells you how much a node is pointed at: how many citations a paper receives, how many followers an account has, or how many regulators act on a gene. A node with in-degree `0` is a source (nothing leads into it). Parallel edges each count, a self-loop counts once, and edge weights are ignored. The graph is not modified. Each call scans the whole edge list, so it takes time proportional to the number of edges. For a summary over many nodes, `get_agg_degree_in()` is more convenient. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node to query, given either as its integer node ID or as its string label (e.g., `3` or `"A"`). A string is always treated as a label. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of incoming edges. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected, or if `node=` is an ID or label that does not exist in the graph. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~get_out_degree`) : Number of outgoing edges. [](`~get_degree`) : Total degree (in-degree plus out-degree). ## Examples {.doc-examples} Both `A` and `C` point to `B`, so `B` has an in-degree of `2`: ::: {#6566fc4b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "B")]) ) graph.get_in_degree("B") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: "A" has no incoming edges at all: ::: {#90143805 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_in_degree("A") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 0 ``` ::: ::: A quick way to find all source nodes is to keep those with in-degree `0`: ::: {#ab1ace38 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} [ graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.get_node_ids() if graph.get_in_degree(nid) == 0 ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['C', 'A'] ``` ::: :::
